prompt: Which statement best describes what "web performance" covers?
explanation: Web performance spans loading (getting the bytes), rendering (turning them into pixels), and runtime responsiveness (reacting to taps, clicks, and scrolling) — not just the initial load time.

options.text: Only how long the page takes to finish loading
Loading, rendering, and how responsive the page is to input after it loads
How visually attractive the design is
The number of features the site has

prompt: Which statements about PERCEIVED performance are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: Perceived performance is the subjective sense of speed; progressive rendering, instant tap feedback, and reserving space all improve it even if raw timings are unchanged. It is not identical to total load time.

options.text: It is how fast the experience feels to the user
It can be improved without changing the raw timings (e.g. with skeletons and instant feedback)
Reserving space so content doesn't jump can improve it
It is exactly the same thing as the total load time

prompt: In the RAIL model, the letter "R" stands for ____ — handling user input quickly.
explanation: RAIL stands for Response, Animation, Idle, and Load. Response is about handling user interactions fast enough that they feel immediate.

prompt: Order these phases as a user experiences them for a fresh page view, from first to last.
explanation: At a high level the browser must receive bytes, render them into visible pixels, and only then can the loaded page respond to interaction.

items.text: The page reacts to a tap or click (runtime responsiveness)

prompt: Match each RAIL goal to what it is about.
explanation: RAIL frames the experience from the user's side: respond to input fast, animate smoothly, use idle time in small pieces, and load meaningful content quickly.

pairs.right: Handle user input quickly so it feels immediate
Produce each frame fast enough to stay smooth
Do non-urgent work in small chunks during idle time
Deliver meaningful, interactive content quickly

prompt: Whose experience should you primarily optimize for?
explanation: A fast dev machine hides the CPU and network costs real users pay. Optimizing for the 75th-percentile real user (typically mobile) reflects what most people actually experience.

options.text: Your own fast laptop on a fast office network
The single fastest visit ever recorded
A realistic 75th-percentile user, often on a mid-range phone and mobile network
Search engine crawlers only

prompt: What is the job of DNS during a page load?
explanation: DNS (Domain Name System) translates a hostname like shop.example.com into the IP address the browser actually connects to. If it isn't cached, that lookup costs a round trip.

options.text: Encrypt the connection between browser and server
Map the site's hostname to a numeric IP address
Compress the HTML before sending it
Decide which images to lazy-load

prompt: Order these steps of a first HTTPS request, from earliest to latest.
explanation: The browser must resolve the name, open a TCP connection, negotiate TLS, send the request, and then wait for the first byte. Each handshake costs a round trip.

items.text: Send the HTTP request for the HTML

prompt: The time from navigation start to the first byte of the response is called ____ (three-letter abbreviation).
explanation: TTFB (Time to First Byte) measures the delay until the first response byte, including DNS, connection setup, TLS, server think time, and travel.

prompt: Which of these are part of TTFB? Select all that apply.
explanation: TTFB bundles redirects, DNS, TCP connect, TLS, server think time, and the first byte's travel. Downloading all images happens later and is not part of TTFB.

options.text: DNS lookup time
TCP and TLS handshake time
The server's processing ("think") time
Downloading every image on the page

prompt: Match each step to what it does.
explanation: Each stage has a distinct job; the two handshakes each cost roughly one network round trip before your HTML can even be requested.

pairs.right: Turn a hostname into an IP address
Open a reliable connection to the server
Set up HTTPS encryption and verify the certificate
Time until the first response byte arrives

prompt: Why does adding a new third-party origin (a different hostname) cost more than it first appears?
explanation: Every brand-new origin pays its own DNS + TCP + TLS setup cost. That's why consolidating origins and using preconnect on the critical ones helps.

options.text: It always doubles your JavaScript size
The browser must do a fresh DNS lookup, TCP handshake, and TLS handshake for that origin before any of its bytes download
It disables HTTP caching for the whole page
It forces the page to reload from scratch

prompt: Why is CSS described as "render-blocking"?
explanation: The browser needs the full CSSOM before it can render, otherwise it would show unstyled content and then restyle it (a FOUC). So slow/large CSS delays the first paint.

options.text: Because the browser won't paint content until it has built the CSSOM, to avoid a flash of unstyled content
Because CSS files are always larger than JavaScript files
Because CSS runs on the GPU
Because CSS can only load after all images

prompt: Put the critical rendering path steps in order.
explanation: The browser builds the DOM and CSSOM, merges the visible parts into a render tree, computes layout, paints pixels, and composites the layers into the final frame.

items.text: Combine them into the render tree

prompt: A plain synchronous <script> is called ____-blocking because it pauses building the DOM until it downloads and runs.
explanation: A synchronous script is parser-blocking: the HTML parser stops constructing the DOM to fetch and execute the script, then resumes.

prompt: Match each script form to when it executes.
explanation: defer preserves order and waits for parsing; async runs opportunistically without order; modules behave like defer by default; a plain script blocks the parser.

pairs.right: Blocks parsing; runs immediately when reached
Runs after parsing finishes, in document order
Runs as soon as it downloads, order not guaranteed
Deferred by default

prompt: Which changes help shorten the critical rendering path for the first paint? Select all that apply.
explanation: Fewer and smaller render-blocking resources, deferred non-critical JS, and inlined critical CSS all shorten the path. Adding more blocking stylesheets does the opposite.

options.text: Defer non-critical scripts instead of blocking in the head
Inline the critical CSS and load the rest without blocking
Add several more render-blocking stylesheets
Reduce the number and size of render-blocking resources

prompt: Which pair of properties can typically be animated at the composite step, without forcing layout or paint?
explanation: transform and opacity can usually be handled by the compositor (often on the GPU) without re-running layout or paint, so they animate smoothly.

options.text: width and top
margin and height
transform and opacity
font-size and padding

prompt: What is the "good" threshold for Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)?
explanation: LCP is good at ≤ 2.5 s, needs improvement up to 4.0 s, and poor above 4.0 s — measured at the 75th percentile of real visits.

options.text: ≤ 1.0 second
≤ 2.5 seconds
≤ 5.0 seconds
≤ 200 milliseconds

prompt: INP became a Core Web Vital in March 2024, replacing the older metric ____ (three-letter abbreviation).
explanation: Interaction to Next Paint (INP) replaced First Input Delay (FID) on March 12, 2024. FID only measured the delay of the first interaction; INP is stricter.

prompt: Which of these are the three Core Web Vitals? Select all that apply.
explanation: The Core Web Vitals are LCP, INP, and CLS. FCP and TTFB are useful related metrics but are not Core Web Vitals.

options.text: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)
Interaction to Next Paint (INP)
Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)
First Contentful Paint (FCP)

prompt: Match each Core Web Vital to its "good" threshold.
explanation: Good bars: LCP ≤ 2.5 s (loading), INP ≤ 200 ms (responsiveness), CLS ≤ 0.1 (visual stability), all at the 75th percentile.

pairs.right: ≤ 2.5 seconds
≤ 200 milliseconds

prompt: An interaction's latency (measured by INP) is made of three parts. Order them as they happen.
explanation: INP = input delay + processing time + presentation delay: the wait before handlers run, the handler work, then painting the visual response.

prompt: What are the units of Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)?
explanation: CLS is unitless — each shift scores impact fraction × distance fraction, and CLS sums the shifts in the worst session window. Good is ≤ 0.1.

options.text: Milliseconds
Pixels
It is a unitless score (impact fraction × distance fraction)
A percentage of the page

prompt: What is "field" (RUM) data?
explanation: Field data (Real User Monitoring) comes from actual users' browsers, reflecting the real spread of devices, networks, and interactions.

options.text: Metrics collected from real users' browsers as they use the site
A single scripted test on a fixed device in a lab
The server's CPU usage
The size of the HTML file

prompt: Match each tool/source to what it is.
explanation: Lighthouse and WebPageTest are lab tools; CrUX and your own web-vitals RUM are field data sources.

pairs.right: A lab audit tool that produces a score and metrics
A lab tool with multi-location waterfalls and filmstrips
A public field dataset reported at the 75th percentile
Your own field RUM measured in real user sessions

prompt: Google's public field dataset from opted-in Chrome users, reported at p75, is the Chrome UX Report, abbreviated ____.
explanation: CrUX (Chrome UX Report) is the public field dataset that powers PageSpeed Insights' field section and Google's page-experience assessment.

prompt: Which statements about LAB data are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: Lab data is a repeatable synthetic test, ideal for debugging and CI. It doesn't measure INP directly (no real user) and isn't collected from real users — that's field data.

options.text: It is controlled and repeatable
It's great for debugging a cause and for catching regressions in CI
It measures INP directly from real interactions
It's collected from thousands of real users

prompt: Which Core Web Vital can a Lighthouse lab run NOT measure directly, using a proxy instead?
explanation: Lighthouse has no real user interacting, so it can't measure INP; it reports TBT as a lab proxy for responsiveness. Confirm INP with field data.

options.text: LCP — it uses FCP instead
CLS — it uses TTFB instead
INP — it uses Total Blocking Time (TBT) as a proxy
It measures all three directly

prompt: Order a healthy measure-and-fix workflow using both data types.
explanation: Use field data to decide what's actually a problem, lab tools to diagnose and iterate quickly, then confirm the real-world effect back in the field.

items.text: Judge the real experience with field data (p75)
Reproduce and diagnose the cause in the lab
Confirm the improvement later in the field

prompt: As of writing, which metric carries the largest weight in the Lighthouse performance score?
explanation: As of writing (Lighthouse 10/11) the weights are FCP 10, SI 10, LCP 25, TBT 30, CLS 25. TBT has the largest single weight, so heavy main-thread JavaScript hurts the score most.

options.text: First Contentful Paint (10%)
Total Blocking Time (30%)
Cumulative Layout Shift (25%)
Speed Index (10%)

prompt: Total Blocking Time is the lab proxy for which Core Web Vital? ____ (three-letter abbreviation).
explanation: Lighthouse can't measure INP without a real user, so it uses TBT (main-thread blocking during load) as the lab proxy for responsiveness.

prompt: Which statements about Lighthouse are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: Lighthouse defaults to a throttled mobile profile, is a lab tool without direct INP, and runs in DevTools/CLI/PSI. A 100 is a lab result and doesn't guarantee good field vitals.

options.text: By default it emulates a mid-tier mobile device with throttling
It is a lab tool and does not measure INP directly
A score of 100 guarantees good field Core Web Vitals
It can run in DevTools, from the CLI, or via PageSpeed Insights

prompt: Match each Lighthouse report section to what it contains.
explanation: Metrics are the numbers; Opportunities estimate savings; Diagnostics give context; Passed audits list what's already good. Savings in Opportunities are estimates.

pairs.right: The measured values (LCP, TBT, CLS, …)
Suggested fixes with estimated time savings
Supporting info like main-thread work and third-party cost
Things the page already does well

prompt: Why doesn't a Lighthouse score of 100 guarantee a good real-world experience?
explanation: The score reflects one throttled lab run and excludes INP (using TBT). Real users span many devices and networks, so field data must confirm the experience.

options.text: Because Lighthouse only tests the homepage
Because it is a lab test on one device profile and doesn't measure INP; real users differ
Because the score ignores LCP
Because 100 is impossible to reach

prompt: Order the Lighthouse score bands from worst to best.
explanation: Lighthouse colours the score 0–49 red, 50–89 orange, and 90–100 green.

prompt: In the Network panel, what does the "Transferred" value represent?
explanation: Transferred is the over-the-wire byte count (after compression); Size is the uncompressed resource. A big gap means good compression, and "(from cache)" means it wasn't downloaded.

options.text: The uncompressed size of the resource on disk
The bytes actually sent over the wire, after compression
The time the request took
The number of requests to that origin

prompt: The Network column that shows WHAT caused a request (so you can trace dependency chains) is the ____ column.
explanation: The Initiator column shows what triggered each request — the HTML or another script — revealing request chains where one resource gates another.

prompt: Which settings help you test a realistic first-visit mobile experience? Select all that apply.
explanation: Disabling the cache simulates a new visitor, and network/CPU throttling mimics a mid-range phone. A warm cache on fast fibre hides the real first-visit cost.

options.text: Turn on "Disable cache"
Apply network throttling (e.g. Slow 4G)
Apply CPU throttling
Test on office fibre with the cache warm

prompt: Order these per-request timing phases as they occur.
explanation: A request queues, resolves DNS, connects (TCP+TLS), waits for the first byte (TTFB), then downloads the content. Setup phases only appear on the first request to an origin.

prompt: Match each Network column to what it tells you.
explanation: Status is the HTTP outcome, Initiator traces chains, Transferred is compressed bytes, and Priority controls ordering.

pairs.right: The HTTP result (200, 304, from cache)
What requested this resource
Bytes sent over the wire (compressed)
The browser's fetch order for the request

prompt: Why turn on "Disable cache" when profiling a page?
explanation: With the cache on, repeat visits show tiny "(from cache)" entries that hide the real cost new visitors pay. Disabling it forces a cold, first-visit load.

options.text: To make the page load faster in the test
To simulate a first-time visitor with an empty cache, revealing the true download cost
To remove images from the page
To disable JavaScript

prompt: What is a performance budget?
explanation: A performance budget is an explicit, shared limit (on timings and/or bytes/requests) that turns speed into an enforceable target so regressions are caught deliberately.

options.text: The money spent on hosting
An agreed limit on metrics and/or resource sizes that the team commits not to exceed
The number of developers on the team
A Lighthouse feature that speeds up the page

prompt: Match each budget concept to its meaning.
explanation: Metric budgets limit outcomes (timings), quantity budgets limit inputs (bytes/requests), score budgets set a minimum tool score, and a regression is an unintended slowdown.

pairs.right: A limit on a timing like LCP or INP
A limit on bytes or request counts
A minimum tool score, e.g. Lighthouse ≥ 90
An unintended slowdown introduced by a change

prompt: A budget only sticks if it's enforced automatically in ____, so a pull request that exceeds a limit fails the build (two letters).
explanation: Enforcing budgets in CI (e.g. Lighthouse CI or a bundle-size check) fails a pull request that breaches a limit, catching regressions before they ship.

prompt: Which are good performance-budget practices? Select all that apply.
explanation: Enforce in CI, budget JS on its own, and anchor to CWV and your real numbers. An always-missed limit trains everyone to ignore the failing check.

options.text: Enforce the budget automatically in CI
Budget JavaScript separately, not just total bytes
Set an aspirational limit you routinely miss
Anchor limits to the Core Web Vitals "good" thresholds and current data

prompt: Why should JavaScript get its own, tighter budget rather than just counting total bytes?
explanation: Byte for byte, JavaScript costs more than images or fonts because after download it is parsed, compiled, and executed on the main thread — so it warrants a dedicated limit.

options.text: JavaScript files are always the largest files
Because JS must be downloaded, parsed, compiled, and executed on the main thread, making it the most expensive kind of byte
Because browsers refuse to cache JavaScript
Because CSS has no cost

prompt: Order the steps of establishing a workable performance budget.
explanation: Start from where you are, set a holdable target, enforce it automatically, then tighten it as the team improves.

items.text: Set a realistic limit anchored to the CWV "good" thresholds
Enforce it in CI so breaches fail the build
Ratchet the limit tighter over time

prompt: Order the four phases that make up LCP.
explanation: LCP = TTFB + resource load delay + resource load time + element render delay. Diagnosing which phase dominates points you to the right fix.

items.text: Resource load delay (before the LCP resource starts loading)
Resource load time (the LCP resource downloads)

prompt: Why should you never add loading="lazy" to the LCP image?
explanation: loading="lazy" defers an image until it's about to scroll into view. The LCP image is already in view and should load eagerly — lazy-loading it directly worsens LCP.

options.text: Because lazy loading corrupts the image
Because it delays loading the very element LCP measures, making LCP worse
Because lazy loading only works on videos
Because it increases the image's file size

prompt: Match each slow LCP phase to the fix that targets it.
explanation: Each phase has a matching fix: CDN for TTFB, early discovery/preload for load delay, image optimization for load time, and removing render-blocking resources for render delay.

pairs.right: Use a CDN and cache at the edge
Preload the image and make it discoverable in the HTML
Use a modern format and correct dimensions
Remove render-blocking CSS/JS

prompt: The HTML attribute that hints a resource should be fetched at high priority is ____ (write it as attribute=value).
explanation: fetchpriority="high" raises a fetch's priority. On the LCP image it helps the browser download it ahead of less important resources.

prompt: Which techniques help the LCP image start downloading earlier? Select all that apply.
explanation: Being in the HTML makes it discoverable, preload starts it early, and fetchpriority raises its priority. loading="lazy" would do the opposite and delay it.

options.text: Put it as a real in the initial HTML
Add <link rel="preload" as="image">
Add fetchpriority="high"
Add loading="lazy"

prompt: If the LCP element is a block of text, what most commonly delays it?
explanation: For text LCP the 'resource' is effectively the font and CSS, so a slow web font or render-blocking CSS delays the text from painting.

options.text: A slow-loading web font and/or render-blocking CSS
The number of images elsewhere on the page
The favicon
Cookies

prompt: What is the most effective way to prevent images from causing layout shift?
explanation: With width/height (or aspect-ratio) the browser knows the aspect ratio and reserves the right space before the image loads, so content below never jumps. Keep height:auto in CSS for responsiveness.

options.text: Load all images with JavaScript
Give each image its width and height attributes (or a CSS aspect-ratio) so space is reserved before it loads
Make every image a background-image
Add loading="lazy" to every image

prompt: Which layout shifts do NOT count toward CLS?
explanation: Shifts within 500 ms of a user interaction are flagged hadRecentInput and treated as expected (e.g. opening an accordion you clicked), so they're excluded from CLS.

options.text: Shifts that happen within 500 ms of a user interaction
Shifts caused by images
Shifts on mobile devices
Shifts in the first second of load

prompt: Which of these are common causes of layout shift? Select all that apply.
explanation: Unsized media, growing slots, and content inserted above existing content all shift the layout. transform/opacity animations do not move other content, so they don't cause shifts.

options.text: Images or videos without dimensions
Ad or embed slots that grow from zero height
Content injected above existing content on load
Animating with transform and opacity

prompt: The CSS property that reserves space for a box in a given width:height ratio (e.g. 16 / 9) is ____.
explanation: CSS aspect-ratio reserves correctly proportioned space for elements without an intrinsic size, such as video embeds, preventing a shift when they load.

prompt: Match each cause of layout shift to its fix.
explanation: Every CLS fix comes down to reserving space (dimensions, min-height) or not displacing existing content (overlays, matched font metrics).

pairs.right: Add width and height attributes
Reserve space with a min-height

pairs.left: Banner injected at top on load
pairs.right: Use a fixed overlay or reserve its space
Match fallback metrics or use font-display: optional

prompt: Order the steps to diagnose and fix a layout shift.
explanation: Record, locate the shifting element, find its cause, apply the reserve-space fix, and confirm CLS improved.

items.text: Record the page load in DevTools
Determine the cause (unsized media, injected content, font)
Reserve space or apply the matching fix

prompt: What does INP measure?
explanation: INP (Interaction to Next Paint) is the responsiveness vital: it measures the latency from an interaction to the next visual update, reporting near the worst interaction of the visit.

options.text: How long the page takes to finish loading
How quickly the page visually responds to interactions like clicks, taps, and key presses
How much the layout shifts
The size of the JavaScript bundle

prompt: Match each part of an interaction's latency to a fix that targets it.
explanation: Input delay is fixed by keeping the main thread free, processing time by doing less work, and presentation delay by making the next frame cheaper to render.

pairs.right: Break up long tasks and yield to the main thread
Do less in the handler; defer non-urgent work
Shrink the DOM and make rendering cheaper

prompt: Main-thread work that runs for more than 50 ms and blocks the page from responding is called a ____ task.
explanation: A long task exceeds 50 ms on the main thread. Because JavaScript is single-threaded there, a long task blocks input until it finishes — the main cause of input delay.

prompt: Which techniques help reduce INP? Select all that apply.
explanation: Breaking up tasks, deferring non-urgent work, and debouncing all keep interactions cheap. Doing everything synchronously in the handler inflates processing time and delays the response.

options.text: Break up long tasks and yield to the main thread
Update the visible UI first, then defer analytics/logging
Debounce or throttle frequently-firing events
Do all work synchronously inside the event handler

prompt: Inside an event handler, which work should run synchronously?
explanation: Do just the visible response synchronously so the user sees a fast reaction, then yield and run non-urgent work (analytics, logging) after the browser paints.

options.text: Only the visible response the user is waiting for; defer the rest
All analytics and logging first, then the UI update
Every possible task, to get it out of the way
Nothing — handlers should be empty

prompt: Order a responsive click handler that avoids blocking the interaction.
explanation: Give feedback first, let the browser paint it, then do heavy work in chunks that yield, and finally run non-urgent work — so the interaction never blocks.

items.text: Show immediate visual feedback (e.g. a spinner)
Yield so the browser can paint that feedback
Do the heavy work in yielding chunks

prompt: Which format is usually the smallest for photographs (with a fallback still recommended)?
explanation: AVIF usually gives the smallest files for photos, with WebP and JPEG as fallbacks (served via <picture>). PNG is for graphics/transparency; GIF should be replaced by video.

options.text: PNG
AVIF
BMP
Animated GIF

prompt: Match each image feature to what it does.
explanation: srcset + sizes let the browser pick the right resolution; <picture> handles format/crop fallback; loading=lazy defers off-screen images.

pairs.right: Lists image sources with width descriptors
Tells the browser how wide the image will display
Provides format fallback or art direction
Defers loading a below-the-fold image

prompt: The HTML element used to offer multiple image formats (with a fallback) or different crops per breakpoint is the ____ element.
explanation: The element wraps several options (by type for format, or media for art direction) plus an fallback.

prompt: Which are good image-optimization practices? Select all that apply.
explanation: Responsive sizes, modern formats with fallback, and set dimensions all help. Lazy-loading the LCP image is the one thing to avoid — it delays LCP.

options.text: Serve responsive sizes with srcset/sizes
Use AVIF/WebP with a JPEG fallback
Always set width and height (or aspect-ratio)
Add loading="lazy" to the LCP image

prompt: Why is PNG a poor choice for photographs?
explanation: PNG is lossless, which bloats photographic content. Photos belong in AVIF/WebP/JPEG; reserve PNG for graphics needing sharp edges or transparency.

options.text: PNG can't be shown in browsers
PNG is lossless and produces very large files for photos; it's meant for graphics/transparency
PNG doesn't support colour
PNG images always cause layout shift

prompt: Order the steps to prepare an optimized photo for the web.
explanation: Pick the format, produce right-sized variants, compress, then write markup that reserves space and sets loading/priority appropriately.

items.text: Choose an efficient format (AVIF/WebP with fallback)
Add width/height and the right loading/priority attributes

prompt: Which web font format should you ship as your primary format?
explanation: WOFF2 has the best compression and is supported across modern browsers, so it's the format to ship — you rarely need others anymore.

options.text: TTF
EOT
WOFF2
SVG fonts

prompt: Match each font-display value to its behaviour.
explanation: block risks invisible text; swap avoids invisible text but can reflow; optional avoids the shift; fallback is a compromise between them.

pairs.right: Hide text briefly (FOIT), then swap in the web font
Show the fallback immediately, then swap (FOUT)
Use the fallback and keep it if the font is slow (best for CLS)
Very short block, short swap window, else keep the fallback

prompt: A font <link rel="preload"> must include the ____ attribute, or the font downloads twice.
explanation: Fonts are fetched in anonymous CORS mode, so a preload without crossorigin doesn't match the real request and causes a duplicate download.

prompt: Which practices reduce the performance impact of web fonts? Select all that apply.
explanation: WOFF2, subsetting, and a correct preload all help. font-display: block leaves text invisible (FOIT) while fonts load, which hurts perceived speed.

options.text: Ship WOFF2
Subset to only the glyphs you use (unicode-range)
Preload the critical font with crossorigin
Use font-display: block on all text so nothing shows until fonts load

prompt: How can you reduce the layout shift (CLS) caused when a fallback font swaps to the web font?
explanation: Matching the fallback's metrics keeps line lengths and heights the same across the swap, and font-display: optional avoids the swap entirely — both cut swap-driven CLS.

options.text: Match the fallback's metrics with size-adjust/ascent-override, or use font-display: optional
Make the font file larger
Remove all fallback fonts
Load the font with JavaScript after everything else

prompt: Order the steps to add a web font with good performance.
explanation: Prepare an efficient, subset WOFF2; declare it with a chosen font-display; preload the critical one (with crossorigin); and stabilize the swap with matched fallback metrics.

items.text: Choose WOFF2 and subset it to needed glyphs
Preload the critical font with crossorigin
Add a metric-matched fallback to reduce swap shift

prompt: What does the Cache-Control directive `no-cache` actually mean?
explanation: `no-cache` still stores the response but requires a revalidation (a conditional request) before reusing it. The directive that means 'never store' is `no-store`.

options.text: Never store the response anywhere
The response may be stored, but must be revalidated with the server before reuse
Cache the response forever
Only cache on the server

prompt: Match each Cache-Control directive to its meaning.
explanation: max-age sets freshness, no-store forbids storing, immutable skips revalidation, and public allows shared caches to store the response.

pairs.right: Fresh (reusable without the network) for N seconds
Never store the response at all
Don't revalidate even on reload — content won't change
Shared caches (CDNs/proxies) may store it

prompt: When a revalidation shows the cached copy is still valid, the server responds with status ____ (the number), sending no body.
explanation: A 304 Not Modified tells the browser its cached copy is still good, so it reuses it without re-downloading the body (though a round trip still happens).

prompt: What's the recommended caching for a fingerprinted asset like app.9f2a1c.js?
explanation: A hashed filename changes when its content changes, so the URL is effectively permanent — cache it for a year and mark it immutable so it's never revalidated.

options.text: no-store
max-age=60
public, max-age=31536000, immutable
no-cache

prompt: Which are good HTTP caching practices? Select all that apply.
explanation: Cache fingerprinted assets long-term, revalidate HTML so deploys are seen, and use public + CDN for shared assets. Caching HTML for a year strands users on old pages.

options.text: Serve fingerprinted assets as immutable for a long time
Serve HTML with no-cache (or a short max-age)
Cache HTML with max-age of one year
Use public + a CDN for shared static assets

prompt: Order what happens when a stale cached file is revalidated and hasn't changed.
explanation: A stale/no-cache resource triggers a conditional request; if the ETag still matches, the server answers 304 and the browser reuses its stored copy without re-downloading.

items.text: The cached copy becomes stale (or is no-cache)
The browser sends a conditional request (If-None-Match with the ETag)
The server sees the content is unchanged
The server returns 304 and the browser reuses its copy

prompt: What is the difference between minification and compression?
explanation: Minification strips whitespace/comments (and shortens JS names) at build time; compression (gzip/Brotli/zstd) reduces the transferred bytes and the browser decompresses them. They're independent and stack.

options.text: They are the same thing with different names
Minification removes source cruft at build time; compression shrinks the bytes in transit and is reversed by the browser
Minification encrypts the file; compression signs it
Compression happens at build time; minification happens on the server

prompt: The request header in which the browser advertises the compression algorithms it supports is ____.
explanation: The browser sends Accept-Encoding (e.g. gzip, br, zstd); the server replies with Content-Encoding naming the algorithm it actually used.

prompt: Which files should you NOT re-compress because they're already compressed? Select all that apply.
explanation: JPEG, WebP/AVIF, and WOFF2 are already compressed — re-compressing wastes CPU for no gain. Text like CSS is highly compressible and should be compressed.

options.text: JPEG images
WebP/AVIF images
WOFF2 fonts
CSS files
